You're welcome. Just remember that while games are fun to develop, at least when you do it as a hobby, they tend to be a worse career option than a pure programmer simply because of how many people that wants to develop games.

As for software development, it is a very large field. A (good) education can help a lot, though there are also a lot that learn by themselves, and whether one gets an education in CS/similar or not one should definitely still learn on one's own as well. Using Android Studio if you want to learn to develop apps is a good idea.

Do note that there is a lot of bullshit in the field of software development as well, and it is a fairly young field still. While I dislike referring to reddit, proggit is still sometimes valuable, as is Hacker News (I do hope to contribute to /v/programming in the future, though I do not have the time or surplus at the moment). Also remember that it really is a very large field - while diving a little into a lot of things as well as diving deeper in a few areas can make excellent sense, there is no way whatsoever to master everything, even if you were a genius never needing sleep studying 24/7 (there is this book from Valve, https://steamcdn-a.akamaihd.net/apps/valve/Valve_NewEmployeeHandbook.pdf, which I am uncertain about how good or bad is, but it talks about "T-shaped" regarding width and depth of knowledge). But there can, at least so far, be very good money in it, especially since doing software development well is not always easy and can be very difficult.

I have trouble giving you good advise, for in some ways, it is an extremely complex field, and there are many issues and challenges both technical and non-technical. One advise I could give is to get an accurate or rather exact understanding of the commonly used subset of the syntax and semantics of the programming language(s) you work with. If you want to work on Android, the typical languages used are Java and possibly also Kotlin. Learning other languages may help you abstract away from particular details. Finding a good learning resource is very useful; learning slightly or somewhat wrong models about the syntax and semantics of a programming language and then (years) later trying to adjust it bit by bit or relearning it is very bothersome and time-consuming - much better to learn it right the first time.

If you are going to learn Java, if you get experienced, I strongly recommend the book "Java: Concurrency in Practice". While it is an older book, it is excellent, and it teaches a number of good things as well as an exact mental model for how to deal with memory consistency on Java/JVM safely. If nothing else, reading and understanding that book should help put you a cut above many or maybe most other Java developers skill-wise (though it is fair from sufficient by itself).

While I am uncertain about how useful it is for Android development in particular, one field that I would recommend learning considerably is functional programming. Very superficially, there have been two main paradigms in CS regarding programming languages and traditions: Imperative programming (Turing machines) and functional programming (lambda calculus). Imperative programming has had the most influence, but functional programming is beginning to have more and more influence due to a number of very good properties and advantages it offers in many cases (for instance, as programs grow older and larger, they can become horribly complex and get all kinds of bad characteristics, some of which have caused companies much harm and problems. Functional programming features, while far from a panacea, can typically help a lot regarding this when used in certain ways). Most mainstream programming languages are adopting more and more features and functionality that are historically seen as being invented in or coming from the functional programming languages, and some functional programming languages are becoming more popular. And it seems that many of the best developers on the forefront of things that were frustrated with the state of things and went looking for better approaches have ended up in functional programming and love it. There are a considerable number of (often older) developers that have not learned it, which hinders their options; I believe that learning it to some degree can be very helpful to you. I am uncertain about which resources to direct you to regarding this. But one advise I will give you is to avoid the purity spiral of only ever using pure functional programming; while in certain cases and circumstances complete functional purity can buy you a lot, it is simply not the best approach open a lot of the time, and imperative programming is still very useful. Also remember that functional programming alone is not really useful; you need general problem solving ability, knowledge about various domains and fields, etc. as well. One book that you might (later on?) find interesting is "Functional Programming in Scala".

Learning a programming language is not in and of itself sufficient - learning how to solve problems using some programming language, whether "small-scale" (algorithmic, like reversing a list, or finding the 3 largest numbers, or proving the correctness of an algorithm or convincing yourself and others that your implementation of some part of the code base covers all possible cases, or the running time of algorithms, etc.) or "large-scale" (creating "architecture" and find requirements, make design, setting up environment and workflow, version control with for instance Git, etc.) is very much needed as well. I am uncertain about which way to point you in regarding this - I think I became much better at the "small-scale" while at university and working with algorithmic courses. I had the book Introduction to Algorithms (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Introduction_to_Algorithms) while at university, but I do not know if I can recommend it for self-study. I have heard good things about the book "Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs", though I have never read it myself. There is also this discussion, where I can recommend reading through the answers, including the one by Madi Connors: https://www.quora.com/Is-Structure-and-Interpretation-of-Computer-Programs-SICP-worth-reading-Is-it-outdated-nowadays.

Finally, while what I say here should be OK, given how complex things are, I would recommend you to take an approach to it (which you may already be doing :-) ) that handles complex situations well, such as seeing recommendations from teachers (I am not a teacher) and see what others do and have success with while holding it up against your own understanding of how to approach learning and developing a career. A final reminder, do remember that there are a lot of bullshit out there and prepare and look into it at least a little bit. Best of luck to you in any case.
